notes.title: 1.1 Basics of English Grammar: The Eight Parts of Speech
notes.content:
• Grammar: the set of rules that govern how words are combined to form correct sentences. Word → phrase → clause → sentence → paragraph.
• Noun: names a person, place, thing, animal, idea or quality.
– Types: proper (Delhi, Anita, Infosys), common (city, girl, company), collective (team, committee, board, jury), abstract (honesty, freedom, management), material (gold, wood), countable (book, laptop) and uncountable (information, advice, furniture, equipment, luggage, news, knowledge).
– Number: singular/ plural — irregular plurals: man–men, child–children, foot–feet, person–people, criterion–criteria, analysis–analyses, datum–data. Gender: masculine, feminine, common, neuter. Case: nominative, objective, possessive. Possessive form: the manager's desk; the managers' room.
• Pronoun: replaces a noun.
– Types: personal (I, you, he, she, it, we, they; me, him, her, us, them), possessive (mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs; my, your, their — determiners), reflexive (myself, himself, themselves), demonstrative (this, that, these, those), interrogative (who, whom, whose, which, what), relative (who, whom, whose, which, that), indefinite (someone, anybody, each, everyone, none), reciprocal (each other, one another), emphatic.
– Rules: use subjective case as subject ("She and I attended"), objective case as object ("between you and me"); a pronoun must agree with its antecedent in number and person.
• Verb: expresses action, occurrence or state of being.
– Types: action verbs (run, write, negotiate); linking verbs (be, seem, become, appear, look, feel); auxiliary (helping) verbs (be, do, have); modal verbs (can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must, ought to); transitive (takes an object: She wrote a report) and intransitive (no object: He arrived); regular (work–worked) and irregular (go–went–gone); finite and non-finite (infinitive, gerund, participle); phrasal verbs (give up, carry out).
– Three principal parts: base form, past simple, past participle (e.g. write–wrote–written).
• Adjective: describes a noun/ pronoun — quality (smart), quantity (some, many), number (five), demonstrative (this), possessive, interrogative. Degrees: positive (tall), comparative (taller), superlative (tallest); more/ most for long adjectives; irregular — good–better–best, bad–worse–worst, far–farther/ further. Order of adjectives: opinion–size–age–shape–colour–origin–material–purpose (a beautiful small old round red Indian wooden table).
• Adverb: modifies a verb, adjective or another adverb — manner (quickly), place (here), time (now), frequency (always), degree (very), reason. Many are formed by adding -ly; adverb vs adjective (fast, hard, late are both).
• Preposition: shows relation between a noun/ pronoun and another word — time (at, on, in, since, for, by, until), place (at, in, on, under, between), direction (to, towards, into), manner/ agent (by, with). Examples: *in* the morning; *on* Monday; *at* 5 pm; *since* 2020; *for* two years; *between* two, *among* many; *good at*, *interested in*, *afraid of*, *depend on*, *different from*, *prefer ... to*.
• Conjunction: joins words, phrases, clauses — coordinating (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so), subordinating (because, although, if, when, while, unless, since), correlative (either…or, neither…nor, both…and, not only…but also, whether…or), conjunctive adverbs (however, therefore, moreover, consequently).
• Interjection: expresses sudden emotion (Oh! Wow! Alas! Hurray!).
• Articles and determiners: a (before consonant sound: a university, a one-rupee note), an (before vowel sound: an hour, an MBA), the (specific/ unique: the sun, the Ganga, the Prime Minister). Omit the article before uncountable general nouns, languages, meals, most proper nouns. Determiners: articles, quantifiers (some, any, much, many, few, a few, little, a little), numbers, possessives, demonstratives.

notes.title: 1.2 Tenses
notes.content:
• Twelve tenses (with examples):
[TABLE]
Tense | Structure | Example
Simple present | V1 (s/es) | She works in a bank.
Present continuous | is/am/are + V-ing | She is working now.
Present perfect | has/have + V3 | She has worked here for 5 years.
Present perfect continuous | has/have been + V-ing | She has been working since morning.
Simple past | V2 | She worked yesterday.
Past continuous | was/were + V-ing | She was working when I called.
Past perfect | had + V3 | She had worked before he arrived.
Past perfect continuous | had been + V-ing | She had been working for two hours.
Simple future | will + V1 | She will work tomorrow.
Future continuous | will be + V-ing | She will be working at 5 pm.
Future perfect | will have + V3 | She will have worked by Friday.
Future perfect continuous | will have been + V-ing | She will have been working for 10 years by June.
[/TABLE]
• Uses: simple present — habits, facts, schedules ("The meeting starts at 10"); present continuous — now, temporary, planned future; present perfect — past action with present relevance (with already, yet, just, ever, never, since, for); simple past — finished action at a definite time; past continuous — action in progress in the past, interrupted action; past perfect — earlier of two past actions; future — predictions, promises, decisions.
• Common mistakes: "I am knowing" ✗ (stative verbs — know, believe, like, want, own — avoid continuous); "He go to office" ✗ → "He goes"; "I have seen him yesterday" ✗ → "I saw him yesterday"; "since two years" ✗ → "for two years"; sequence of tenses — "I thought he is honest" ✗ → "was honest".

notes.title: 1.3 Subject–Verb Agreement
notes.content:
• Rule: a singular subject takes a singular verb; a plural subject takes a plural verb.
• Key rules:
– Two subjects joined by and take a plural verb ("Tea and coffee are available") — but if they form one idea, singular ("Bread and butter is my breakfast").
– Subjects joined by or / nor / either…or / neither…nor — verb agrees with the nearer subject ("Neither the manager nor the employees were present").
– Collective nouns — singular when acting as a unit ("The committee has decided"), plural when members act individually ("The committee are divided").
– Each, every, either, neither, everyone, anybody, nobody, someone — singular.
– A number of + plural verb; the number of + singular verb.
– Uncountable nouns (information, advice, news, furniture) — singular. Plural in form but singular in meaning — news, mathematics, economics, physics.
– Expressions like along with, as well as, together with, in addition to do not change the number of the subject: "The manager, along with his team, is attending."
– Quantities/ money/ time as a unit — singular ("Ten lakh rupees is a big amount").
– Relative clauses: "He is one of the employees who are efficient."
– Inverted sentences — verb agrees with the real subject ("There are many reasons").

notes.title: 1.4 Construction of Sentences
notes.content:
• Sentence: a group of words that expresses a complete thought with a subject and a predicate; starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop, question mark or exclamation mark.
• Phrase: a group of words without a subject–verb pair (in the morning, very quickly). Clause: a group of words with a subject and a verb — independent (main) clause (can stand alone) and dependent (subordinate) clause (cannot stand alone) — noun, adjective and adverb clauses.
• By function: declarative (statement), interrogative (question), imperative (command/ request), exclamatory (emotion), plus optative (wish).
• By structure:
– Simple sentence: one independent clause ("The company launched a new product.").
– Compound sentence: two or more independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction or semicolon ("The company launched a product, and sales increased.").
– Complex sentence: one independent + one or more dependent clauses ("Because the demand was high, the company increased production.").
– Compound-complex sentence: two or more independent + at least one dependent clause.
• Sentence patterns: SV (Prices rose.), SVO (She wrote the report.), SVC (He is a manager.), SVA (The meeting is in the boardroom.), SVOO (She gave him a gift.), SVOC (They elected him chairman.).
• Characteristics of a good sentence: clarity, unity, coherence, conciseness, correct word order, parallel structure (parallelism — "She likes reading, writing and travelling", not "to travel"), variety, emphasis.
• Common sentence errors: fragment (incomplete sentence), run-on/ fused sentence, comma splice, dangling modifier ("Walking down the road, the bus hit him" ✗), misplaced modifier ("She nearly drove for two hours"), double negative, redundancy ("return back", "free gift"), wordiness.
• Active and passive voice: active — subject performs the action ("The manager approved the plan"); passive — subject receives the action ("The plan was approved by the manager"). Formation: be + V3. Tense changes: is approving → is being approved; approved → was approved; has approved → has been approved; will approve → will be approved; can approve → can be approved. Use passive when the doer is unknown or unimportant ("The office was robbed").
• Direct and indirect speech: direct — exact words in quotes; indirect — reported. Changes: pronouns, tense (backshift — simple present → simple past; present continuous → past continuous; will → would; can → could), words of time/ place (now → then; today → that day; tomorrow → the next day; here → there; this → that). Examples: He said, "I am busy." → He said that he was busy. She asked, "Where do you live?" → She asked where I lived. He said, "Close the door." → He ordered them to close the door.
• Conditionals: zero (If you heat ice, it melts), first (If it rains, we will cancel), second (If I were the CEO, I would...), third (If I had known, I would have attended).
• Modals: can/ could (ability, permission), may/ might (possibility), must (obligation), should (advice), would (polite request), shall (offer: "Shall I open the window?").

notes.title: 1.5 Punctuation
notes.content:
• Full stop (.) — ends a statement; abbreviations (Mr., Dr.).
• Comma (,) — separates items in a list; after introductory phrases ("However, ..."); before coordinating conjunction joining independent clauses; around non-essential clauses; in dates and addresses; with direct speech. Do not put a comma between subject and verb; avoid comma splice.
• Semicolon (;) — joins two closely related independent clauses; separates complex list items.
• Colon (:) — introduces a list, explanation or quotation ("You need three things: ...").
• Question mark (?) — ends a direct question. Exclamation mark (!) — shows strong emotion; avoid it in formal business writing.
• Apostrophe (') — possession (the company's policy; employees' benefits) and contraction (don't, it's = it is). Its (possessive) vs it's (it is).
• Quotation marks (" ") — direct speech, titles, special terms.
• Hyphen (-) — compound words (well-known, state-of-the-art); dash (—) — a break or emphasis; parentheses ( ) — extra information; brackets [ ]; ellipsis (...) — omission; slash (/) — alternatives.
• Capitalisation: first word of a sentence; proper nouns; days, months; titles; the pronoun "I"; headings.
• Spelling: commonly confused words — affect/ effect, accept/ except, principal/ principle, stationary/ stationery, complement/ compliment, advice/ advise, there/ their/ they're, lose/ loose, than/ then, its/ it's, whose/ who's, council/ counsel, personal/ personnel, formally/ formerly, ensure/ insure/ assure.

notes.title: 2.1 Paragraph Writing: Structure and Qualities
notes.content:
• Paragraph: a group of related sentences developing one main idea. Usually 5–10 sentences (about 100–200 words).
• Parts: Topic sentence (states the main idea — usually the first sentence); supporting sentences (explanations, examples, facts, statistics, reasons); concluding (closing) sentence (summarises or links to the next idea).
• Qualities: unity (all sentences relate to the main idea), coherence (logical flow; transitions; repeating key words; pronouns; parallel structure), completeness (adequate development), emphasis, clarity and conciseness, variety in sentence length.
• Transitions (linking words): addition (also, moreover, in addition), contrast (however, but, although, on the other hand), cause/ effect (therefore, as a result, because), sequence (first, next, finally), example (for instance, for example), conclusion (in conclusion, to sum up).
• Methods of developing a paragraph: examples, facts and statistics, comparison/ contrast, cause and effect, definition, classification, process, description, narration, reasons.
• Steps: (1) choose the topic; (2) identify the purpose and audience; (3) write the topic sentence; (4) brainstorm supporting points; (5) arrange logically; (6) write the draft; (7) revise and edit.

notes.title: 2.2 Paragraph Styles: Descriptive, Narrative, Expository and Persuasive
notes.content:
• 1. Descriptive paragraph: paints a picture in words of a person, place, object or experience using sensory details (sight, sound, smell, taste, touch), vivid adjectives and figurative language; follows spatial order (top to bottom, left to right, near to far).
– Sample: "The old railway station at dawn is a world of its own. Pale sunlight spills across the rusted tracks, and the smell of hot tea drifts from the corner stall. Porters in faded red shirts hurry along the platform while a lone vendor calls out in a rhythmic chant. The air hums with the promise of journeys about to begin."
• 2. Narrative paragraph: tells a story or recounts events in chronological order with characters, setting, plot; uses past tense and time transitions (first, then, later, finally); has a point or lesson.
– Sample: "Last summer, I took my first job as an intern at a small start-up. On the opening day I was so nervous that I spilled coffee on my shirt. My supervisor smiled, handed me a napkin and said, 'We have all been there.' By the end of the week, I had learnt the team's workflow, and by the end of the month, I had delivered my first report. That experience taught me that confidence comes from action."
• 3. Expository paragraph: explains, informs or defines — gives facts, process, cause–effect, comparison; objective tone; uses logical order and signal words.
– Sample: "Digital payments have transformed how people in India transact. The Unified Payments Interface (UPI) lets users transfer money instantly using a mobile number. First, the user links a bank account to a payment app. Next, the user sends or receives money by entering a virtual address and a PIN. As a result, cash use has fallen in many cities, and small shops now accept payments through a simple QR code."
• 4. Persuasive paragraph: convinces the reader to accept an opinion or take action; clear claim (stance), reasons/ evidence, appeals (logic, emotion, credibility), addresses counter-argument, strong call to action.
– Sample: "Every company should adopt a four-day work week. Studies show that employees who work fewer days are more productive and less stressed. Shorter weeks also reduce commuting costs and energy use. Critics argue that output will fall, but trials in several countries show that output stayed steady while satisfaction rose. Therefore, employers who want healthier, more loyal teams should begin pilot programmes now."
• Comparison:
[TABLE]
Type | Purpose | Order | Language
Descriptive | Create a picture | Spatial | Sensory, vivid adjectives
Narrative | Tell a story | Chronological | Past tense, time words
Expository | Explain/ inform | Logical | Facts, neutral, signal words
Persuasive | Convince/ motivate | Order of importance | Strong claims, evidence, call to action
[/TABLE]

notes.title: 2.3 Essay Writing
notes.content:
• Essay: a short, organised piece of non-fiction writing on a single topic, expressing the writer's ideas with a clear structure. Typical length 300–1,000 words.
• Structure:
– Introduction: hook (question, quotation, fact, anecdote), background/ context, thesis statement (the central argument in one sentence).
– Body paragraphs (3–4): each with a topic sentence, evidence, explanation and link to the thesis.
– Conclusion: restate the thesis in new words; summarise key points; end with a closing thought, recommendation or call to action; do not introduce new points.
• Types of essays: descriptive, narrative, expository, argumentative/ persuasive (also reflective, analytical, compare-and-contrast, cause-and-effect, definition, problem–solution; formal vs informal/ personal; business essays).
• Writing process: 1. Pre-writing (brainstorm, mind map, research, outline) → 2. Drafting → 3. Revising (content, organisation) → 4. Editing (grammar, style) → 5. Proofreading (spelling and punctuation) → 6. Publishing/ submitting.
• Thesis statement: a specific, debatable, one-sentence claim ("Remote work improves productivity and employee wellbeing, so firms should adopt hybrid models.") — not a fact or a question.
• Sample essay outline — "Role of Social Media in Business":
– Introduction: hook — "Today, a single post can make or break a brand"; thesis — social media gives businesses powerful marketing tools but requires careful management.
– Body 1: reach and customer engagement. Body 2: low-cost marketing and brand building. Body 3: risks — misinformation, reputation damage, privacy.
– Conclusion: restate the thesis; businesses must plan and monitor to benefit.
• Style tips: use simple, precise words; vary sentence length; active voice; avoid slang, clichés and contractions in formal essays; keep to the word limit; maintain a consistent tone and tense; cite sources (avoid plagiarism).
• Common errors: vague thesis, poor transitions, one-sided argument, repetition, long paragraphs, grammatical errors.
• Essay vs report vs article: essay — personal argument; report — factual and formal; article — written for publication.

notes.title: 3.1 Reading Skills and Strategies
notes.content:
• Reading comprehension: the ability to read, understand, interpret and evaluate a text.
• Levels of comprehension: literal (what is directly stated), inferential (what is implied — reading between the lines), evaluative/ critical (judging the text), appreciative/ creative (responding to style and ideas).
• Types of reading:
– Skimming: rapid reading to get the general idea (headings, first and last lines of paragraphs) — e.g. reading a newspaper headline.
– Scanning: searching for specific information (name, date, number) without reading everything — e.g. finding a phone number.
– Intensive reading: careful, detailed reading of short texts for full understanding (study, contracts).
– Extensive reading: reading longer texts for pleasure/ general understanding (novels, magazines).
– Critical reading: analysing the author's purpose, bias and evidence.
– Silent vs oral reading; speed reading.
• Reading strategies:
– Preview the text (title, headings, images, abstract); predict; set a purpose; annotate (underline, margin notes); summarise each paragraph; question; infer from context; visualise; monitor comprehension; re-read difficult parts.
– SQ3R method: Survey (preview), Question (turn headings into questions), Read, Recite (recall in own words), Review.
– Guessing word meaning from context: use clues — synonyms, antonyms, examples, definitions, word parts (prefix, root, suffix).
• Improving reading speed and comprehension: read daily; increase vocabulary; avoid subvocalisation and regression; use a pointer; chunk words; read varied material.

notes.title: 3.2 Genres and Difficulty Levels
notes.content:
• Genres of text:
– Fiction: short stories, novels, fables, fantasy, science fiction, mystery; elements — plot, characters, setting, theme, tone.
– Non-fiction: biographies, autobiographies, memoirs, essays, travelogues, speeches, self-help.
– News and journalism: news reports (inverted pyramid — who, what, when, where, why, how), editorials (opinion), features, columns, letters to the editor.
– Academic/ scientific texts: research papers, textbooks, abstracts — formal, technical, objective, citations.
– Business and professional texts: emails, memos, reports, proposals, case studies, annual reports, contracts, press releases, product manuals.
– Poetry and drama: imagery, figurative language, rhythm.
– Persuasive/ advertising texts: slogans, ads, brochures, opinion pieces.
– Digital texts: blogs, social media, websites, infographics.
• Difficulty levels: basic/ elementary (simple vocabulary, short sentences, direct facts), intermediate (some complex sentences, inferencing, wider vocabulary), advanced (long sentences, abstract ideas, specialised vocabulary, implied meaning, critical reasoning). Factors affecting difficulty: vocabulary, sentence length and structure, abstractness, familiarity with the topic, organisation, length, cultural background, tone (irony, satire).
• Features of different tones: formal, informal, humorous, serious, optimistic, pessimistic, sarcastic, objective, critical, neutral.

notes.title: 3.3 Answering Comprehension Questions
notes.content:
• Question types: factual/ literal (who, what, when), inferential (why, what does it suggest), vocabulary in context (meaning of a word), main idea/ title, author's purpose and tone, true/ false/ not given, multiple choice, sequencing, summary, reference questions (what does "it" refer to?), critical evaluation (fact vs opinion; bias).
• Steps: (1) read the passage once for the gist; (2) read the questions; (3) re-read to find answers; (4) answer in your own words in complete sentences; (5) check grammar and word limit.
• Main idea: the central point of the passage; supporting details: facts and examples; inference: a conclusion based on clues and prior knowledge; fact vs opinion: fact can be proved; opinion is a belief (words like *should*, *best*, *I think*).
• Author's purpose: to inform, persuade, entertain, describe, instruct. Tone clues: word choice (adjectives, adverbs), figurative language.
• Mini-passage practice (sample for revision):
– Passage A: "Rohan arrived at the interview twenty minutes early. He reviewed his notes calmly, greeted the receptionist politely and waited. When called in, he answered each question with confidence." Q: What can we infer about Rohan? — He is well-prepared, disciplined and confident.
– Passage B: "The company's profit rose by 12% in the third quarter, mainly due to higher exports, although costs also increased by 5%." Q: What caused the profit growth? — Higher exports.
– Passage C: "Renewable energy, once considered expensive, is now the cheapest source of power in many regions, and countries are rapidly expanding solar and wind farms." Main idea: renewable energy has become affordable and is expanding.
• Common errors: copying whole lines; answering from outside knowledge; ignoring the question word; ignoring word limit; wrong inference; not checking the title.
• Business reading: how to read a report (executive summary first, then findings, conclusion, recommendations), a contract (clauses, definitions, penalty), annual report (MD&A, balance sheet, notes), email chain (latest message, action items).

notes.group_name: Unit 4: Speaking Skills: Vocabulary, Dialogue Writing and Storytelling
notes.title: 4.1 Vocabulary Development
notes.content:
• Vocabulary: the set of words a person knows and uses. Types: active (productive) — words used in speaking and writing; passive (receptive) — words understood but not used.
• Why it matters: clear expression, confidence in speaking, better reading comprehension, professional impression, accuracy.
• Word-formation:
– Root words, prefixes and suffixes: *un-* (unhappy), *re-* (rebuild), *dis-* (disagree), *mis-* (misunderstand), *pre-* (prepare), *inter-* (interact), *-tion* (decision), *-ment* (management), *-ness* (kindness), *-able* (reliable), *-ful* (helpful), *-less* (useless). Latin/ Greek roots: *bene* (good — benefit), *mal* (bad — malfunction), *port* (carry — transport), *dict* (say — dictate), *graph* (write — autograph), *scrib/ script* (write — describe, manuscript), *spect* (see — inspect), *aud* (hear — audience), *cred* (believe — credit, credible), *vert* (turn — convert).
– Word families: decide, decision, decisive, decisively; compounding (blackboard); conversion (a "run" / to "run").
• Relationships between words: synonyms (similar meaning — big/ large; buy/ purchase), antonyms (opposite — expand/ contract), homophones (same sound, different spelling — their/ there; right/ write), homonyms (same spelling/ sound, different meaning — bank), homographs, hyponyms, collocations, word associations, connotation vs denotation, register (formal/ informal).
• Collocations: words that go together — make a decision, take a risk, do business, meet a deadline, heavy rain, strong tea, launch a product, close a deal, draw a conclusion.
• Idioms (examples): break the ice (start a conversation), bite the bullet (face a difficulty), a blessing in disguise, back to square one, cut corners, hit the nail on the head, in the red (in debt), once in a blue moon, the ball is in your court, spill the beans, under the weather, think outside the box, on the same page.
• Phrasal verbs (business): set up (establish), carry out (perform), call off (cancel), bring up (raise a topic), look into (investigate), follow up, take over, put off (postpone), run out of, come up with, turn down (reject), figure out, step down, wind up.
• One-word substitutes: autobiography (life story written by oneself), anonymous (of unknown name), bibliophile (lover of books), omnipresent (present everywhere), unanimous (agreed by all), orphan, optimist, amateur, monopoly (exclusive control), novice (beginner), philanthropist (lover of mankind), inevitable (cannot be avoided), posthumous (after death), pedestrian.
• Business vocabulary: revenue, profit, turnover, liability, asset, equity, dividend, stakeholder, merger, acquisition, negotiation, procurement, logistics, outsourcing, benchmark, deadline, deliverable, agenda, quorum, minutes, bottom line, ROI, leverage, scalability, KPI, brand equity.
• Commonly confused words: affect/effect, adapt/adopt, beside/besides, continual/ continuous, eminent/ imminent, farther/ further, historic/ historical, lie/ lay, precede/ proceed.
• Ways to build vocabulary: read widely (newspapers, books, business magazines); keep a vocabulary notebook/ flashcards; use a dictionary (meaning, pronunciation, usage, part of speech) and thesaurus (alternatives — with care); learn words in context; use new words in speaking and writing within 24–48 hours; spaced repetition; word games; listen to podcasts; learn roots; group words by theme.
• Pronunciation: syllables and stress (PROduct noun vs proDUCE verb), intonation (rising for yes/no question; falling for statements), silent letters (knife, hour, debt, receipt), schwa sound; clarity, pace, pause.

notes.group_name: Unit 4: Speaking Skills: Vocabulary, Dialogue Writing and Storytelling
notes.title: 4.2 Dialogue Writing
notes.content:
• Dialogue: a conversation between two or more people written down. Purpose: to show how people speak and interact; used in plays, stories, language practice, business role plays.
• Format (script style): speaker's name followed by a colon, then the speech; each speaker begins a new line; stage directions in brackets; conversational, natural language; short sentences.
• Rules/ tips:
– Each speaker's lines start on a new line.
– Use simple, natural language — contractions are acceptable in informal dialogue (it's, don't).
– Keep it short, relevant and purposeful (greeting → main topic → conclusion).
– Use polite expressions in formal dialogues (Could you please..., Would you mind...).
– Show turn-taking — question and answer, reaction.
– Opening — greeting and introduction; middle — discussion; closing — thanks/ goodbyes.
– Maintain a consistent tone (formal for business, informal for friends); avoid long monologues.
– In narrative dialogue (fiction) use quotation marks and tags (said, asked) and a new paragraph for each speaker.
• Useful expressions: greeting (Good morning, nice to meet you), asking (Could you tell me..., May I know...), agreeing (Absolutely, I agree), disagreeing politely (I see your point, but...), suggesting (How about..., Why don't we...), apologising (I'm sorry for the inconvenience), closing (Thank you for your time).
• Sample 1 — Dialogue between a customer and a bank officer:
– Customer: Good morning. I would like to open a savings account.
– Officer: Good morning, sir. Certainly. May I have your Aadhaar card and PAN card for KYC?
– Customer: Here you go. Is there a minimum balance requirement?
– Officer: Yes, the minimum balance is Rs 1,000. Would you also like a debit card and mobile banking?
– Customer: Yes, please. How long will it take?
– Officer: The account will be active within a day. Please sign here.
– Customer: Thank you for your help.
– Officer: You are welcome. Have a great day!
• Sample 2 — Dialogue between two colleagues on a project deadline:
– Riya: Hi Arjun, did you finish the market analysis?
– Arjun: Almost. I need one more day to compile the survey data.
– Riya: The client presentation is on Friday, so we have limited time. Can I help?
– Arjun: That would be great. Could you prepare the charts?
– Riya: Sure. I'll send them by tomorrow noon.
– Arjun: Perfect. Let's meet on Thursday morning to review everything.
• Types of dialogues: formal (interview, meeting, customer service, negotiation), informal (friends, family), telephone, persuasive, problem–solution, sales (seller–buyer), complaint.
• Sample 3 — Complaint dialogue (formal): Customer: "I received a damaged phone." Support: "I am sorry to hear that. May I have your order number?" ... closing with a replacement.

notes.group_name: Unit 4: Speaking Skills: Vocabulary, Dialogue Writing and Storytelling
notes.title: 4.3 Storytelling
notes.content:
• Storytelling: the art of narrating events with characters, setting and plot to engage and communicate a message — oral, written or visual.
• Elements of a story: characters (protagonist, antagonist), setting (time and place), plot (sequence of events), conflict (problem), climax (turning point), resolution (outcome), theme (central message), point of view (first person, third person), tone/ mood.
• Story structure: beginning (exposition) → rising action → climax → falling action → resolution (denouement) (Freytag's pyramid); three-act structure; hero's journey (Joseph Campbell).
• Techniques: start with a hook; use vivid sensory language ("show, don't tell"); dialogue; suspense; emotion; pace; humour; repetition; metaphors/ similes; a clear message; an ending that resonates.
• Oral storytelling delivery: voice modulation (pitch, volume, pace), pauses, facial expressions and gestures, eye contact, posture, movement, use of props, audience interaction, practising and timing.
• Business storytelling: used in branding (Tata's trust story), sales pitches, leadership (vision stories), presentations, interviews (STAR method: Situation, Task, Action, Result), case studies, customer testimonials. Structure: Context → Challenge → Action → Result → Lesson.
• Sample short story (moral): "The Honest Shopkeeper. Ramesh ran a small grocery in a village. One evening a customer paid Rs 500 instead of Rs 50 and left in a hurry. Ramesh closed his shop, walked two kilometres to the customer's home and returned the money. The customer was moved and told the whole village. Soon more customers came to Ramesh's shop, and his business grew. Moral: honesty builds trust, and trust builds business."
• Tips: know your audience; keep it simple and short; have one message; make characters relatable; use concrete details; end with a lesson; practise aloud; rehearse timing; vary tone; handle nervousness by deep breathing.
• Speaking skills (general): fluency, accuracy, clarity, confidence; avoid fillers (um, you know); use the rule of three; active listening; body language; audience awareness; structure (opening–body–closing).

notes.title: 5.1 Meaning, Importance and Principles of Business Etiquette
notes.content:
• Etiquette: the accepted code of polite, respectful and professional behaviour in a social or professional setting. Business etiquette: the unwritten rules of behaviour that help people interact professionally, build trust and create a positive image.
• Importance: creates a positive first impression; builds trust and relationships; improves teamwork and communication; reflects the organisation's culture and brand; avoids misunderstandings and conflict; helps in career growth; supports cross-cultural business; boosts confidence.
• Core principles: respect, courtesy, punctuality, honesty and integrity, professionalism, discretion/ confidentiality, consideration, accountability, good listening, cultural sensitivity, appropriate communication.
• Etiquette vs manners vs protocol: manners — general social politeness; etiquette — situational rules; protocol — formal rules (diplomatic, ceremonial).
• First impressions: formed in the first 7–30 seconds from appearance, body language, handshake, greeting, tone.
• Greetings and introductions: stand up, smile, make eye contact, firm (not crushing) handshake (about 2–3 seconds), state your name and role clearly. Order of introduction: introduce a junior to a senior, a colleague to a client, a younger to an older person (in Indian context respect for seniority), a man to a woman in traditional etiquette but in business the rank rule prevails. Business card etiquette: present with both hands (in many Asian countries), read it, treat it with respect, do not write on it in front of the giver, keep in a card holder. Namaste/ bowing and cultural greetings. Addressing: use titles (Mr., Ms., Dr., Prof.) until invited to use first names.
• Body language (non-verbal): posture, eye contact, gestures, facial expressions, personal space (proxemics — social distance about 1.2–3.5 m), tone of voice. Avoid: crossed arms, fidgeting, pointing, slouching, looking at the phone.
• Cross-cultural etiquette: high-context (Japan, India, China — indirect, relationship) vs low-context (USA, Germany — direct, explicit) cultures; punctuality (Germany strict; India flexible but expected in business); gift giving (Japan — both hands; avoid gifts in sets of four; China — avoid clocks); left hand considered unclean in many cultures; eye contact; titles and hierarchy; Hofstede dimensions; respect dietary and religious practices.

notes.title: 5.2 Email Etiquette
notes.content:
• Subject line: clear, specific and short ("Meeting rescheduled to 3 pm, Friday"); never blank.
• Salutation: "Dear Mr. Rao," (formal), "Hello Anita," (semi-formal); closing: "Yours sincerely"/ "Best regards"/ "Kind regards" + name, designation, contact.
• Content: be brief, clear, and purposeful; one main topic; short paragraphs; bullet points for lists; polite tone; state the request or action and deadline; proofread for spelling and grammar.
• To, Cc, Bcc: To — main recipients; Cc — for information; Bcc — hidden copy (privacy for large groups). Reply all only when necessary. Forward carefully.
• Tone: avoid ALL CAPS (shouting), excessive exclamation marks, emojis (in formal), slang, sarcasm; do not write when angry; be respectful in complaints.
• Attachments: mention them in the body; use clear file names; compress large files; check before sending.
• Response time: reply within 24 hours (or acknowledge); use an out-of-office reply; do not send confidential data by email without protection; signature professional; avoid chain mails and spam.
• Email vs other channels: use calls for urgent/ sensitive matters.
• Sample professional email:
– Subject: Request for Meeting — Project Review. Dear Mr. Sharma, I hope this email finds you well. I would like to schedule a meeting to review the project's progress. Would Thursday at 11 am suit you? Please let me know if another time is more convenient. Thank you for your time. Kind regards, Meera Nair, Project Manager.
• Netiquette (internet etiquette): respect privacy, avoid cyberbullying, verify before sharing, think before you post, professional social-media presence (LinkedIn), do not discuss confidential matters in public.

notes.title: 5.3 Telephone Etiquette
notes.content:
• Answering a call: answer within 2–3 rings; greet and identify ("Good morning, Infosys, Anita speaking. How may I help you?"); smile (it affects the voice); speak clearly, at moderate pace and tone; listen actively; avoid eating or chewing.
• Making a call: plan the purpose; call at a suitable time; identify yourself and the reason; ask "Is this a good time?"; keep it short; take notes.
• Putting a caller on hold: ask permission ("May I put you on hold for a moment?"); thank for waiting; do not keep callers holding long; transfer correctly — tell the caller where you are transferring.
• Taking messages: record caller's name, company, number, time/ date, message, action needed; repeat to confirm.
• Handling difficult callers: stay calm, listen, apologise where appropriate, avoid arguing, offer solutions, escalate if needed.
• Closing: summarise action points; thank the caller; let the caller hang up first; never hang up abruptly.
• Mobile phone etiquette: keep it on silent in meetings; step out to take calls; avoid loud ringtones; do not use speaker in public spaces; avoid texting during conversations; voicemail greeting professional.
• Useful phrases: "May I know who is calling?"; "Could you please spell that?"; "I am afraid he is not available"; "Can I take a message?"; "Thank you for calling."

notes.title: 5.4 Dining Etiquette
notes.content:
• Before the meal: arrive on time; follow the dress code; wait for the host to seat guests/ begin; napkin on the lap (after the host); turn off the phone.
• Seating and ordering: wait to be seated; order moderately priced items; avoid messy dishes; follow the host's lead on courses; tell about dietary restrictions earlier.
• Table manners: use cutlery from the outside in; bread plate on the left, glass on the right ("BMW": bread, meal, water — left to right); no elbows on the table; chew with the mouth closed; don't talk with food in the mouth; pass dishes to the right; take small bites; do not blow on hot food; rest cutlery on the plate; place cutlery together (4 o'clock position) when finished; do not reach across; do not use a toothpick at the table.
• Conversation: light topics; avoid politics, religion, personal matters; do business after ordering or at the end as per the host; include everyone; listen.
• Paying the bill: the host pays; if you invited, you pay; thank the host; tip appropriately; follow-up thank-you note.
• Indian context: vegetarian/ non-vegetarian preferences; eating with the right hand where customary; washing hands; respect for elders — wait for them to start; cross-cultural — avoid beef/ pork assumptions; do not waste food.
• Alcohol: drink only if appropriate; limit consumption; no pressure.

notes.title: 5.5 Office, Cubicle, Dress and Meeting Etiquette
notes.content:
• Office etiquette: punctuality (arrive before time); respect for colleagues and hierarchy; greet colleagues; keep the workplace clean; respect personal space; do not gossip; use "please/ thank you/ excuse me"; confidentiality; respect time and deadlines; dress appropriately; use shared resources responsibly (printer, pantry, meeting rooms); respect diversity and avoid discrimination and harassment (POSH Act, 2013 — prevention of sexual harassment); be a team player; honour commitments; proper use of internet/ social media.
• Cubicle (open-plan) etiquette: keep noise low (calls, music with headphones); do not enter without knocking/ "knocking" on the cubicle wall; no strong food smells; respect "do not disturb" signs; keep the desk tidy; do not touch others' belongings; avoid loud conversations/ speaker calls — use meeting rooms; avoid eavesdropping; moderate perfume; keep phone on silent; do not shout over cubicle walls; use chat.
• Dress code: formal (suit/ saree/ salwar-kameez/ shirt-trousers, formal shoes), business casual, smart casual, casual Friday, uniform. Guidelines: clean, ironed, well-fitted clothes; modest; minimal jewellery and fragrance; neat grooming (hair, nails); appropriate footwear; adapt to the company/ occasion/ culture; avoid ripped, revealing or flashy clothes; colours — navy, grey, black, white are safe; dress for the role you want. Interview — formal. Video-call dress — professional from top to bottom.
• Meeting etiquette:
– Before: agenda circulated; purpose clear; invite relevant people; be on time; prepare; book the room; send pre-reads.
– During: arrive early; silence phones; take notes; listen; don't interrupt; raise your hand/ speak when invited; stay on the topic and time; chair keeps order; respect all opinions; avoid side conversations and multitasking; greet and introduce; summarise decisions and assign actions.
– After: circulate the minutes (decisions, responsible persons, deadlines) within 24 hours; follow up on actions.
– Virtual meetings: test the technology; mute when not speaking; camera on if required; neutral background; good lighting; use the chat/ "raise hand" feature; look at the camera; avoid eating; join on time; share the screen carefully; record only with permission.
– Role of chair and participants; quorum; agenda; minutes.
• Other etiquette: lift/ elevator, corridor, restroom etiquette; gift and gratitude; thank-you notes; handling criticism; apologising; social-media etiquette; email-signature; business travel etiquette; networking (conference, LinkedIn); visiting a client's office; hosting guests (greet, offer water/ tea, escort); parking and vehicle courtesy; interview etiquette; respect for support staff.

notes.group_name: Unit 6: Logical Thinking: Logic, Rhetoric — Ethos, Pathos and Logos
notes.title: 6.1 Fundamentals of Logic
notes.content:
• Logic: the science of correct reasoning — the study of the principles of valid inference and argument. Aristotle is the father of logic (the *Organon*).
• Statement (proposition): a sentence that is either true or false (not a question, command or exclamation).
• Argument: a set of statements in which premises (reasons/ evidence) are offered in support of a conclusion. Indicator words: premise — because, since, as, for; conclusion — therefore, thus, hence, so, consequently.
• Standard form: Premise 1; Premise 2; Therefore, Conclusion.
• Deductive reasoning: moves from general to specific; if the premises are true and the argument is valid, the conclusion must be true (certainty). Example: "All employees must wear ID badges. Ravi is an employee. Therefore, Ravi must wear an ID badge."
• Inductive reasoning: moves from specific observations to a general conclusion; the conclusion is probable, not certain. Example: "The sun has risen every day so far; therefore the sun will rise tomorrow." Types: generalisation, analogy, causal inference, prediction.
• Abductive reasoning: inference to the best explanation.
• Validity vs soundness: an argument is valid if the conclusion follows from the premises (the form is correct); sound if it is valid and all premises are true. An argument can be valid but unsound ("All birds can fly; penguins are birds; so penguins can fly" — valid in form but a false premise). Strong/ weak (inductive) and cogent (strong with true premises).
• Syllogism: a deductive argument with two premises and a conclusion (major premise, minor premise, conclusion) with three terms (major, minor, middle). Categorical propositions: A (All S are P), E (No S is P), I (Some S are P), O (Some S are not P). Example: All managers are leaders (major). Anita is a manager (minor). Therefore, Anita is a leader (conclusion). Rules: the middle term must be distributed at least once; no term may be distributed in the conclusion unless distributed in the premises; two negative premises give no conclusion; two particular premises give no conclusion.
• Hypothetical syllogism: If P then Q; if Q then R; therefore if P then R. Disjunctive syllogism: P or Q; not P; therefore Q. Modus ponens: If P then Q; P; therefore Q. Modus tollens: If P then Q; not Q; therefore not P.
• Fallacies of formal logic: affirming the consequent (If P then Q; Q; therefore P ✗) and denying the antecedent (If P then Q; not P; therefore not Q ✗).
• Logical connectives: and (∧), or (∨), not (¬), if…then (→), if and only if (↔). Truth table of implication: P → Q is false only when P is true and Q is false.
• Necessary vs sufficient condition: A is sufficient for B if A guarantees B; A is necessary for B if B cannot occur without A.
• Critical thinking skills: analysing arguments, identifying assumptions, evaluating evidence, distinguishing fact from opinion, spotting bias, considering alternatives, drawing sound conclusions; Socratic questioning; Bloom's taxonomy.
• Logic in business: decision making, negotiations, audits, problem solving, data interpretation, ethics.

notes.group_name: Unit 6: Logical Thinking: Logic, Rhetoric — Ethos, Pathos and Logos
notes.title: 6.2 Informal Fallacies
notes.content:
• Fallacy: an error in reasoning that makes an argument unsound or invalid.
[TABLE]
Fallacy | Description | Example
Ad hominem | Attacking the person, not the argument | "You can't trust his proposal; he failed last year."
Straw man | Misrepresenting the opponent's view to attack it | "She wants flexible hours, so she wants no discipline at all."
False dilemma (either/or) | Presenting only two options | "Either we cut salaries or we shut down."
Slippery slope | Claiming a small step leads to extreme outcomes without evidence | "If we allow casual Fridays, soon nobody will dress properly."
Appeal to authority | Accepting a claim because an authority says so (irrelevant authority) | "A film star endorses this loan scheme, so it's safe."
Bandwagon (ad populum) | "Everyone does it, so it's right" | "Millions use this app, so it must be secure."
Circular reasoning (begging the question) | Conclusion assumed in the premise | "He is honest because he never lies."
Red herring | Diverting to an irrelevant issue | "Why discuss pollution when unemployment is high?"
Hasty generalisation | Conclusion from too small a sample | "Two customers complained, so the product is bad."
Post hoc (false cause) | Assuming that because B followed A, A caused B | "Sales rose after the new logo, so the logo caused it."
Appeal to emotion | Using feelings instead of reasons | "Think of the poor children — you must donate to our firm."
Tu quoque | "You also do it" | "You tell me to save, but you spend too."
Appeal to ignorance | True because it hasn't been disproved | "No one has proved ghosts don't exist, so they do."
Equivocation | Using a word with two meanings | "A feather is light; what is light cannot be dark; so a feather cannot be dark."
Genetic fallacy | Judging by origin | "That idea came from a rival, so it's wrong."
Loaded question | Question with a built-in assumption | "Have you stopped cheating?"
Composition/ division | Assuming parts and whole share properties | "The team is excellent, so every member is excellent."
Appeal to tradition | "We have always done it" | "We've always filed manually, so continue."
Anecdotal evidence | Personal story instead of data | "My uncle smoked and lived to 90."
[/TABLE]
• How to avoid fallacies: check relevance, sufficiency and acceptability of premises; look for hidden assumptions; stay on the issue; use enough, representative evidence.

notes.group_name: Unit 6: Logical Thinking: Logic, Rhetoric — Ethos, Pathos and Logos
notes.title: 6.3 Rhetoric — Ethos, Pathos and Logos
notes.content:
• Rhetoric: the art of effective, persuasive communication, in speech or writing (Aristotle's *Rhetoric*). Its goal is to persuade or inform a particular audience in a particular situation.
• Aristotle's three modes (appeals) of persuasion:
– Ethos (credibility/ character): appeal to the speaker's credibility, authority, trustworthiness and ethics. Ways: qualifications and experience, expertise, reputation, honesty, fairness, citing reliable sources, professional tone, shared values. Example: "As a doctor with twenty years of experience, I recommend regular exercise." Weakness: can be misused through false authority.
– Pathos (emotion): appeal to the audience's emotions — fear, pity, joy, anger, hope, pride, guilt. Ways: stories, vivid imagery, emotive words, personal anecdotes, music, pictures. Example: an advertisement showing a hungry child to seek donations. Weakness: can manipulate and ignore reasoning.
– Logos (logic/ reason): appeal to reason, logic, facts, statistics, evidence, definitions, analogies, cause–effect reasoning. Example: "Studies show that a 10% reduction in energy use saves Rs 5 lakh a year." Weakness: can be dry and may fail to move people.
• Kairos: the right time/ occasion for the appeal (the fourth appeal added by later scholars); Telos: purpose.
• Rhetorical situation / triangle: speaker (writer), audience, message (text), plus context, purpose and medium. Rhetorical devices: repetition, rhetorical question, metaphor, simile, alliteration, anaphora, antithesis, hyperbole, rule of three, irony, analogy, parallelism.
• Effective persuasion uses a balance of all three — credible speaker (ethos), emotionally engaged audience (pathos), and sound reasoning (logos). Examples: Martin Luther King Jr.'s "I Have a Dream" (all three), advertisements, political speeches, Gandhi's speeches.
• Ad examples: a toothpaste advertisement — "9 out of 10 dentists recommend" (ethos + logos); a charity advertisement with a crying child (pathos); a car advertisement with safety ratings (logos), a celebrity (ethos), a happy family (pathos).

notes.group_name: Unit 6: Logical Thinking: Logic, Rhetoric — Ethos, Pathos and Logos
notes.title: 6.4 Picture Description and Analysis of Ethos, Pathos and Logos
notes.content:
• Purpose: to describe an image in words and analyse how it persuades through ethos, pathos and logos (as in advertisements, posters, photographs, cartoons).
• Steps for picture description:
– 1. Observe: look at the whole picture (overall impression), then details — people, objects, setting, colours, expressions, text, layout, background, lighting, focal point.
– 2. Describe objectively: *"The picture shows..."* — foreground, middle ground, background; left/ right/ centre; use the present tense; use precise adjectives and prepositions of place (in the centre, on the left, behind).
– 3. Interpret the message and mood: purpose, audience, tone, symbolism, colours (red — urgency/ passion; blue — trust/ calm; green — nature/ growth; black — power/ seriousness).
– 4. Analyse the appeals:
  – Ethos: brand marks and logos, experts, certifications, testimonials, celebrity, the credibility of the organisation.
  – Pathos: emotional images, faces, children, animals, music, colours, slogans arousing feelings.
  – Logos: facts, numbers, graphs, product features, comparisons, logical claims.
– 5. Evaluate effectiveness: is the balance appropriate? Is it manipulative? Who is the target? What is missing?
– 6. Write the paragraph/ essay: introduction (what the picture is and its purpose), description, analysis of ethos, pathos, logos, conclusion (overall effectiveness).
• Useful phrases: "The image depicts...", "In the foreground we can see...", "The colour red conveys...", "The advertiser appeals to the viewer's emotions by...", "The use of statistics lends the message credibility...", "This establishes trust (ethos) because...".
• Sample 1 — Picture: a charity poster showing a thin child holding an empty bowl, with the text "Rs 50 feeds a child for a day. Donate now. Registered NGO — 80G certified."
– Description: In the centre, a thin child with large eyes holds an empty steel bowl against a dull background. The text at the bottom gives a donation amount and an NGO tag. The dim colours create a sombre mood.
– Pathos: the child's gaze and empty bowl evoke pity and guilt and prompt action. Logos: the specific figure "Rs 50 feeds a child" gives a clear, logical cost–benefit. Ethos: "Registered NGO — 80G certified" assures the donor of the organisation's legitimacy.
– Evaluation: emotional force is strong, but the poster could add data on outcomes to strengthen logos.
• Sample 2 — Picture: a smartwatch advertisement showing a smiling athlete at sunrise and the text "Track your health. 7-day battery. Recommended by cardiologists."
– Description: The athlete jogs along a beach with the sun rising behind; the watch is in the foreground. Pathos: the sunrise and smile suggest health, energy, and aspiration. Logos: "7-day battery" is a verifiable feature; Ethos: "Recommended by cardiologists" — expert endorsement.
• Sample 3 — Picture: a bank advertisement showing a family in front of a new home with the text "Home loans at 8.5%. Trusted by 10 lakh families since 1980."
– Pathos: the family's joy and the home evoke security and pride; Logos: a specific interest rate; Ethos: a long history and number of customers.
• Writing a paragraph on ethos, pathos and logos in a picture (model): "The advertisement uses all three appeals. First, it builds credibility (ethos) through the doctor's endorsement and the hospital's logo. Second, it appeals to emotion (pathos) through the image of a grandmother laughing with her grandchildren, which suggests that good health means more time with loved ones. Finally, it uses logic (logos) by citing that regular screening reduces risk by 40%. Together, the appeals make the message balanced and persuasive."

notes.title: 7.1 Debating as a Rhetorical Strategy
notes.content:
• Debate: a structured, rule-governed discussion in which two sides present opposing arguments on a motion (resolution) to persuade an audience/ judges. Not a quarrel — focuses on reasoned argument, evidence, rebuttal and respectful exchange.
• Debating as a rhetorical strategy: uses ethos, pathos and logos; builds critical thinking, research, public speaking, listening, teamwork, quick thinking, confidence and persuasion; trains one to see both sides of an issue; used in law, politics, business negotiations, boardrooms, media, academia.
• Motion types: Fact/ definition ("This house believes that AI will replace most jobs"), value ("TH believes privacy is more important than security"), policy ("This house would ban single-use plastic"). Phrases: "This House Believes (THB)", "This House Would (THW)", "This House Regrets (THR)", "This House Supports."
• Sides: Proposition (Government/ Affirmative/ For) — supports the motion and must define it; Opposition (Negative/ Against) — rejects it. Burden of proof lies on the proposition.
• Formats:
– Parliamentary (British Parliamentary — BP): four teams (Opening Government, Opening Opposition, Closing Government, Closing Opposition) of two; roles — Prime Minister, Leader of Opposition, Deputy PM, Deputy LO, Member of Government, Member of Opposition, Government Whip, Opposition Whip; speeches of 7 minutes; Points of Information (POIs) allowed between the 2nd and 6th minutes.
– Asian Parliamentary: two teams of three; reply speeches; 7 minutes.
– Oxford-style: an audience votes before and after the debate.
– Lincoln–Douglas: one-on-one, value-focused; Public Forum; Policy debate (team, evidence-heavy); Karl Popper (cross-examination); World Schools style; Cross-examination debate.
• Structure of a speech: Introduction (greeting, define/ signpost), Body (arguments: claim–reason–evidence–impact), Rebuttal, Conclusion (summarise, closing line).

notes.title: 7.2 Constructing Arguments and Rebuttals
notes.content:
• Toulmin model: Claim (the position), Grounds/ Data (evidence), Warrant (link between data and claim), Backing, Qualifier, Rebuttal.
• PEEL/ CREI structure: Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link (or Claim, Reason, Evidence, Impact). Types of evidence: statistics, expert opinion, case studies/ examples, analogies, historical facts, logic.
• Case building: define the motion; set the framework/ model; 2–3 substantive arguments; anticipate opposition; prepare rebuttals; signpost.
• Rebuttal: identify the opponent's point → state your counter → give reason/ evidence → explain the impact. Techniques: deny (factual error), turn (use their argument against them), outweigh (acknowledge, but it matters less), show irrelevance, show logical gap, expose a fallacy.
• Points of Information (POIs): brief interruptions (15 seconds) by the opposing side — accept 1–2, politely decline others ("No thank you"); the questioner says "On that point"; offer sharp, short POIs.
• Flowing (note-taking): record the arguments and responses in columns to track.
• Delivery: clear voice, moderate pace, eye contact, gestures, confidence, time management.
• Adjudication criteria: Matter (content, logic, evidence), Manner (delivery, style), Method (structure, role fulfilment), Rebuttal/ Engagement.
• Preparation tips: research both sides; understand terms; pick strong arguments rather than many; practise; keep to time; listen carefully.

notes.title: 7.3 How to Moderate a Debate
notes.content:
• Moderator (chair): a neutral facilitator who manages the process — does not take sides.
• Responsibilities:
– Before: understand the motion and format; prepare the rules and time limits; coordinate with timekeepers and judges; set up the room and the speaking order; brief the speakers.
– Opening: welcome the audience; introduce the motion, the teams, the judges and the rules; explain timing signals and POI rules.
– During: call speakers in order; enforce time limits (bell/ cards); maintain decorum — stop interruptions and personal attacks; ensure equal opportunity; keep the discussion on topic; manage POIs; remain impartial in tone and body language; handle disruptions calmly and firmly; clarify rules if disputes arise; monitor audience behaviour.
– Q&A/ open floor: invite questions; ensure fairness; avoid long statements; paraphrase unclear questions.
– Closing: thank participants; summarise (neutrally); announce adjudication/ voting procedures; declare results (if required) and close with courtesy.
• Qualities of a good moderator: neutrality, fairness, authority with politeness, knowledge of the format, time sense, active listening, clear voice, tact, quick thinking, respectful, composed under pressure.
• Common challenges: dominating speakers; overshooting time; personal attacks; off-topic remarks; hostile audience; technical glitches (online debates); bias perception. Solutions: set ground rules; polite firmness; use timers; redirect the topic.

notes.title: 7.4 Ethics of Debating
notes.content:
• Principles:
– Respect for opponents and the audience — attack arguments, not people.
– Honesty and integrity — no fabrication of facts or data; cite sources; do not misquote.
– Fairness and following the rules — time limits, format and judges' decisions.
– Truth-seeking over winning at all costs.
– Open-mindedness and willingness to listen/ learn.
– Avoid fallacies, manipulation, bullying, intimidation and offensive language.
– Responsibility — avoid spreading misinformation; consider the impact on vulnerable groups.
– Confidentiality, courtesy, sportsmanship — accept results gracefully; shake hands.
– Transparency of evidence; avoid cherry-picking.
• Ethical vs unethical tactics: ethical — strong evidence, logical rebuttal, clear structure; unethical — personal attacks, distortion, shouting down, "gish gallop" (overwhelming with many weak points), misrepresenting opponents, hidden agenda.
• Debate and democracy: debate promotes free speech, accountability and informed decisions.

notes.title: 7.5 Both-Side-Ism, Fallacy of Relativism and Principle of Charity
notes.content:
• Both-side-ism (false balance, false equivalence): the practice of presenting two sides of an issue as equally valid or equally supported by evidence, even when the evidence strongly favours one side; often seen in media (e.g. giving equal time to a climate-change denier and a scientist consensus). Problems: misleads audiences; gives undue legitimacy to fringe views; ignores weight of evidence; confuses "fairness" with "equal time."
– Healthy alternative: present different perspectives while indicating where evidence lies; use "weight of evidence" approach; distinguish empirical questions (settled by evidence) from value questions (legitimate disagreement).
– Note: debate training requires arguing either side, which is a skill exercise and not a claim that both sides are equal; the judge's role is to assess the quality of argument.
• Fallacy of relativism (relativist fallacy): the mistaken belief that "all views/ truths are equally valid" or "truth is relative to each person", therefore no view can be judged right or wrong. Types: subjective relativism ("What is true for you is true for you"), cultural relativism taken to extremes ("every culture's practice is right for that culture, so no practice can be criticised"). Why a fallacy: it is self-defeating (the claim "all truth is relative" is itself claimed to be true absolutely); confuses differences in opinion with absence of truth; blocks reasoned debate and critical evaluation.
– Correct view: some questions have objective answers (facts about the world); differences in belief do not make all beliefs equally justified; respect for people does not mean agreement with every claim. (Distinguish tolerance of persons from acceptance of all ideas.) Also related to moral relativism and epistemic relativism.
• Principle of Charity: when interpreting an opponent's statement or argument, assume the most reasonable, rational and strongest version of it — give the benefit of doubt — before criticising. Associated with Neil Wilson, W.V.O. Quine, Donald Davidson; in argumentation it is the opposite of the straw man.
– Steel-manning: reconstruct the opponent's argument in its strongest form, then answer it. Rapoport's rules (Daniel Dennett): (1) restate the opponent's position so clearly that they say "I wish I'd put it that way"; (2) list points of agreement; (3) mention what you learned; (4) only then rebut or criticise.
– Benefits: reduces misunderstanding; builds trust and civility; improves the quality of debate; makes rebuttals stronger and fairer; promotes learning; helps negotiation and conflict resolution.
– Limits: charity doesn't mean accepting bad arguments, pretending a fallacy isn't one, or ignoring clear intent; apply reasonable charity.
– Charity vs straw man: straw man — distort to defeat easily; charity — strengthen to engage honestly.
[TABLE]
Concept | Meaning | Key risk/ benefit
Both-side-ism | Treating unequal positions as equal | Gives false legitimacy to weak claims
Relativism fallacy | "All views are equally valid" | Self-defeating; blocks critical thinking
Principle of charity | Interpreting opponents at their strongest | Improves fairness and quality of debate
Straw man | Distorting opponent's argument | Bad faith, misleading
[/TABLE]
• Sample short debate (motion: "This House believes that remote work should be the default for office jobs."):
– Proposition (PM): "Honourable judges, we define remote work as ... Our first argument is productivity: surveys show higher output and fewer commutes... Our second argument is inclusion: ...". Opposition (LO): "We accept the definition, but remote work harms collaboration and mentoring... The proposition ignores junior employees." Rebuttal (principle of charity): "The opposition's strongest point is mentoring; however, hybrid mentoring programmes address this." Closing: summary and call to the judges.

notes.title: 8.1 Planning a Project Presentation
notes.content:
• Presentation: a structured oral (and visual) communication of information, ideas or findings to an audience to inform, persuade or demonstrate.
• Steps in planning:
– 1. Define the purpose (inform, persuade, demonstrate, report) and the objective (what should the audience know/ do after?).
– 2. Analyse the audience (size, knowledge, expectations, culture, interests, level of formality).
– 3. Research and gather content (data, examples, visuals, reliable sources).
– 4. Organise the content (logical flow; main points; rule of three).
– 5. Prepare visual aids (slides, charts, models, demos).
– 6. Prepare delivery (script/ notes, timing, rehearsal).
– 7. Check venue and equipment (projector, microphone, laptop, remote, backups).
– 8. Plan for questions.
• Time planning: rule — about 1–2 minutes per slide; opening 10%, body 80%, closing 10%.
• Project presentation (academic/ business): presents a project's problem, objectives, method, findings and recommendations — e.g. a market research project, feasibility study, business plan, case study, internship report, product launch.

notes.title: 8.2 Structure and Content of the Presentation
notes.content:
• Standard structure (Tell them what you'll say; say it; tell them what you said):
– Opening: greeting, hook (question, story, fact, quote, statistic), introduce yourself/ team, topic and objective, agenda/ roadmap.
– Body: 3–5 key points, each with evidence, examples and visuals; transitions ("Moving on to...", "As we can see...").
– Closing: summary of key points; conclusion/ recommendations; call to action; thank you and invitation for questions.
• Typical project presentation outline (slide-by-slide):
[TABLE]
Slide | Content
1 | Title slide — project title, names, course/ organisation, date
2 | Agenda/ outline
3 | Introduction/ background and problem statement
4 | Objectives (and scope)
5 | Literature/ context (brief)
6 | Methodology — data sources, sample, tools
7–9 | Findings/ analysis — charts, tables, key insights
10 | Discussion — interpretation, implications
11 | Conclusion and recommendations
12 | Limitations and future scope
13 | Thank you / Q&A
14 | References/ appendix
[/TABLE]
• Storytelling in presentations: problem → solution → benefits; use stories and analogies; connect with the audience.
• Sample presentation topic: "Analysing UPI Adoption among College Students" — Problem: limited understanding of digital payment behaviour; Objective: study the extent and reasons for UPI usage; Method: a survey of 100 students; Findings: 92% use UPI daily; top reasons — convenience and cashback; main concern — fraud; Conclusion: adoption is high but fraud awareness must improve; Recommendation: run awareness workshops.

notes.title: 8.3 Designing Slides and Using Visual Aids
notes.content:
• Slide design principles:
– Keep it simple: one idea per slide; minimal text (about 6 lines × 6 words — the "6×6 rule"; avoid reading slides aloud).
– Readable fonts: sans-serif (Arial, Calibri), minimum 24-pt body text, 32–44 pt titles; high contrast (dark text on a light background or vice versa); consistent theme, fonts and colours.
– Use visuals: charts (bar — comparison, line — trend, pie — proportion), images, icons, diagrams, flowcharts, infographics, videos (short). Label charts clearly; cite sources.
– Avoid: clutter, too many colours, heavy animation, low-quality images, copyright violations, spelling errors.
– Guy Kawasaki's 10-20-30 rule: 10 slides, 20 minutes, 30-point minimum font (for pitch).
– Layout: alignment, white space, rule of thirds, visual hierarchy.
– Colour psychology: blue — trust; green — growth; red — urgency; avoid red-green combos (colour-blind).
• Other visual aids: whiteboard, handouts, flip charts, models, props, demonstrations, posters.
• Tools: Microsoft PowerPoint, Google Slides, Canva, Keynote, Prezi, Pitch; Excel for charts; Mentimeter for polls; speaker notes and presenter view.
• Accessibility: alt-text, large font, captions, colour-blind-friendly palette.

notes.title: 8.4 Delivery, Group Presentations and Q&A
notes.content:
• Delivery skills:
– Verbal: clear voice, moderate pace, volume, pauses, emphasis, avoid fillers, simple language, vary tone.
– Non-verbal: eye contact (scan the room), posture, purposeful gestures, movement, facial expressions, smile; do not turn your back or read from slides.
– Confidence: practise out loud (3+ rehearsals), record yourself, time yourself; arrive early; breathing exercises; positive self-talk; know your first minute by heart.
– Handling nervousness: preparation, deep breathing, visualisation, start with a story, connect with friendly faces, drink water, accept the nervous energy as enthusiasm.
– Engaging the audience: questions, polls, stories, examples, humour (appropriate), interaction, demos.
– Handling technical issues: backup (USB, cloud), PDF copy, adapters, a plan B without slides.
• Group presentations:
– Roles: coordinator/ leader, researcher, designer, speaker(s), timekeeper, Q&A responders.
– Planning: divide sections by strengths; agree on a common template; set deadlines; rehearse together for transitions and timing; introduce each other and hand over smoothly ("Now my colleague Rahul will explain...").
– Do's: all members speak; be consistent in style; support each other during Q&A; avoid contradicting teammates; stand attentively when not speaking.
– Don'ts: unequal speaking time; reading from the slides; arguing in front of the audience; unprepared handovers.
• Question and answer (Q&A) session:
– Prepare likely questions; listen to the full question; pause; repeat/ paraphrase the question; answer briefly and honestly; if you don't know, say so and offer to follow up; stay calm and polite with hostile questions; direct to the right team member; thank the questioner; manage time; end with a strong closing statement.
• Evaluation criteria (rubric): content and research (30%), organisation and structure (20%), visual design (15%), delivery and communication (20%), teamwork (5%), time management (5%), Q&A handling (5%) (weights vary).
• Feedback: seek and use feedback; self-evaluation; peer review; reflection.
• Professional ethics: acknowledge sources (avoid plagiarism); use data honestly; respect copyright; confidentiality of data/ respondents.
• Presentation checklist: objective clear; audience analysed; structure ready; slides simple; backup saved; rehearsed with timing; handouts; Q&A prepared; dress professionally; arrive early.
